title: UTOPIA 2100: An Agent-Based Model of a Martian Workforce

context_sources.name: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, occupational employment 2011-2015

limitations: The birth-probability formula is split across lines and reconstructed from the prose.
The investment identity is garbled; the zero-income debt term is read from the prose.
The tax-bracket table has its rows shifted relative to the rates.
The equality metric breaks the squared gap across two lines.
The sensitivity table has its notes detached from the population rows.
The printed NetLogo source runs many pages and is not re-executed here.

tasks: Define parameters for income, education and equality
Simulate ten years of jobs, schooling and income
Balance a wage distribution between productivity and wellbeing
Test a hundred-year run and an emergency evacuation

section_map.summary: Agent model, three metrics, a $70,000 floor.
Even sex split, mean age 37, one innovator in ten.
Mandatory college, retirement at 70, no families.
One named agent climbs a degree and job ladder.
BLS shares, percentile interpolation, 4.65 per year.
Tuned birth curve and Canadian inflation.
Five tax brackets and a closed economy.
Income, education and equality, with earthly benchmarks.
Floor at $70,000, leave at 10 and 3 months.
Innovator-heavy populations fail; emergencies scale linearly.

contributions.summary: A spread penalty that peaks at a target gap and replaces the quadratic Gini coefficient.
A wage floor chosen where the income metric peaks even though output keeps rising.
An evacuation test that refuses to choose who arrives.

dependency_graph.handoff: Agent incomes and employment status feed the tax, the transfers and the accounts
The inflation path deflates wages, savings and investment
Incomes, unemployment and gender shares by occupation are the raw material of the three metrics
The income metric picks the wage floor and the leave, and all three metrics rank the populations

assumptions.summary: Mandatory associate's degree, retirement at 70, life expectancy 100.
No family network, and death independent of income.
No trade, and a fixed interest rate.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Five years of BLS data fit exponentially and scaled to 2100.
Two censored incomes replaced by the cap of 187,200.

models.summary: An agent life cycle with percentile pay.
A tuned birth curve and two-cycle inflation.
Sweeps over the floor, leave, founding mix and emergency size.

verification.summary: Every founding population converges to the same age shape.
Unemployment settles near 3 to 4 percent for all six mixes.

results_trace.summary: Income metric peaks at a $70,000 floor while output is still rising.
Raising the tax rate from 30 to 90 percent cuts debt from $2.44 billion to $0.28 billion and investment with it.
Emergency output scales linearly up to 100,000 arrivals.

writing_logic.summary: Differential equations are considered and rejected before the agent model is introduced.
The Gini coefficient is defined and then declined on cost grounds.
A flat leave sweep is read as freedom to choose for happiness.

language_observations.summary: The entire mechanism is narrated as the life of one named person.
A data source is swapped, and the reason is the source country's temperament.
The chosen policy is the peak of one column, not the top of the other.
The conclusion closes on a borrowed tag line.

visualization_observations.summary: Figure 1: flowchart of an agent's life.
US inflation, 1923 to 2012, shown as too erratic to extrapolate.
Historical inflation series treated as roughly sinusoidal.
Figure 2: raw normal age draw beside the folded founding distribution.
Figure 3: age distribution at three points across 100 years.
Figure 4: education metric dropping, then spiking.
Table sweeping the wage floor against the income metric and output.
Table sweeping maternity and paternity leave against the income metric.
Table of tax rate against the income metric and government debt.
Table of tax rate against innovator investment.
Table 1: education requirement and worker growth by occupation.
Table 2: income level and income growth by occupation.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: The birth curve is built to peak at 26 and then scaled to a target rate.
The equality target of 3.5 is stated with no derivation.
Leave lengths are chosen on an unmodeled happiness gain.

weaknesses.summary: Eighty years of compounding from five years of census data.
Single stochastic runs are reported where the authors say averages are needed.
Infrastructure, the binding constraint in an evacuation, is outside the model.

independent_extensions.summary: Add a household network for inheritance and transfers.
Make physical capacity a constraint on emergency size.
Optimize the tax dial instead of only sweeping it.

candidate_rule_impacts.summary: Set the wage floor at the peak of the welfare metric, not at the peak of output.
Economic absorption scales with headcount; physical capacity does not.

unresolved_questions.question: Which overall tax rate should the colony actually adopt?
Where does the equality target of 3.5 come from?
At what arrival size does infrastructure fail?
